{{short description|American chemist}}
'''James R. Heath''' (born 1962) is an American chemist and the president and professor of Institute of Systems Biology.<ref name="ISB">{{cite web|title=ISB Appoints James Heath as President|url=https://www.systemsbiology.org/news/2017/04/03/institute-systems-biology-recruits-technology-pioneer-james-heath-president/|website=ISB|date=3 April 2017 |accessdate=3 April 2017}}</ref> Previous to this, he was the Elizabeth W. Gilloon Professor of Chemistry at the [[California Institute of Technology]], after having moved from [[University of California, Los Angeles|University of California Los Angeles]].<ref name="Caltech">{{cite web|title=James R. Heath|url=https://www.cce.caltech.edu/content/james-r-heath|website=Caltech|accessdate=19 July 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160309014651/https://www.cce.caltech.edu/content/james-r-heath|archive-date=2016-03-09|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Early years ==
Heath graduated with a degree in Chemistry in 1984 from [[Baylor University]] in Texas, where he was an active member of the [[NoZe Brotherhood]]. He completed his Ph.D. in Physics and Chemistry from [[Rice University]] in 1988.<ref name="Caltech"/>

== Academic career ==
From 1988 to 1991, he was a [[Miller Research Fellows|Miller Research Fellow]] at the Department of Chemistry, [[University of California, Berkeley]]. From 1991 to 1994, he was a Research Staff Member at IBM T.J. Watson Research Laboratory in [[Yorktown, New York]].<ref name="Academies">{{cite book|last1=Academies|first1=Chemical Sciences Roundtable, Board on Chemical Sciences and Technology, Division on Earth and Life Studies, National Research Council of the National|title=Reducing the time from basic research to innovation in the chemical sciences : a workshop report to the Chemical Sciences Roundtable|date=2003|publisher=National Academies Press|location=Washington, D.C.|isbn=0-309-08734-1|page=56|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Gq_wfBemQdUC&pg=PA56}}</ref> He joined the faculty at [[UCLA]] in 1994 and became Professor of Chemistry in 1997. He founded the [[California NanoSystems Institute]] in 2000 and served as its Director until  moving to become the Elizabeth W. Gilloon Professor of Chemistry at [[Caltech]].

== Research ==
Heath's academic work has focused on [[quantum phase transition]]s and developed architectures, devices, and circuits for molecular electronics. More recently, his work has moved towards applying expertise in nanoscale and molecular systems to addressing problems in cancer and infectious diseases.

When Heath was a graduate student at [[Rice University]], he ran the experimental apparatus that generated the first [[Fullerene|C<sub>60</sub> molecules]] and, ultimately, won the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] for the three senior members of the collaboration: [[Robert F. Curl]] and [[Richard E. Smalley]] of [[Rice University]] and [[Harold Kroto]] of the [[University of Sussex]]. This research is significant for the discovery of a new [[Allotropy|allotrope]] of carbon known as a [[fullerene]].  Other [[allotropes of carbon]] include [[graphite]], [[diamond]] and [[graphene]]. James R. Heath's 1985 paper entitled "C60:  Buckminsterfullerene", published with colleagues  Harry Kroto, S. C. O’Brien, R. F. Curl, and R. E. Smalley, was honored by a Citation for Chemical Breakthrough Award from the Division of History of Chemistry of the American Chemical Society, presented to Rice University in 2015.<ref name="Award">{{cite web|title= 2015 Awardees|url=http://www.scs.illinois.edu/~mainzv/HIST/awards/CCB-2015_Awardees.php|website=American Chemical Society, Division of the History of Chemistry|publisher=University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign School of Chemical Sciences|date=2015|accessdate=1 July 2016}}</ref><ref name="Breakthrough">{{cite web|title=Citation for Chemical Breakthrough Award|url=http://www.scs.illinois.edu/~mainzv/HIST/awards/Citations/2015-Kroto%20plaque.pdf|website=American Chemical Society, Division of the History of Chemistry|publisher=University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign School of Chemical Sciences|date=2015|accessdate=1 July 2016}}</ref>
<ref name="C60 publication">{{cite journal|last1=Kroto|first1=H. W.|last2=Heath|first2=J. R.|last3=O'Brien|first3=S. C.|last4=Curl|first4=R. F.|last5=Smalley|first5=R. E.|title=C60: Buckminsterfullerene|journal=Nature|date=14 November 1985|volume=318|issue=6042|pages=162–163|doi=10.1038/318162a0|bibcode=1985Natur.318..162K |s2cid=4314237}}</ref> The discovery of fullerenes was recognized in 2010 by the designation of a [[National Historic Chemical Landmarks|National Historic Chemical Landmark]] by the [[American Chemical Society]] at the Richard E. Smalley Institute for Nanoscale Science and Technology at Rice University in Houston, Texas.<ref name="ChemLandmark">{{cite web|title=Discovery of Fullerenes National Historic Chemical Landmark|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/education/whatischemistry/landmarks/fullerenes.html|website=American Chemical Society|accessdate=18 July 2016}}</ref>

Heath is known for publishing an architecture demonstration of molecular computers, or moletronics. In moletronics, single molecules serve as switches, "quantum wires" a few atoms thick serve as wiring, and the hardware is synthesized chemically from the bottom up. It was published in the summer of 1999 by Heath, J. [[Fraser Stoddart]] (at the time at UCLA) and their collaborators in the journal ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]''.<ref name="Collier">{{cite journal|last1=Collier|first1=C. P.|first2=E.W. |last2=Wong|first3= M. |last3=Belohradsky|first4= F.J. |last4=Raymo|first5= J.F. |last5=Stoddart|first6= P.J. |last6=Kuekes|first7= R.S. |last7=Williams|first8= J.R. |last8=Heath
|title=Electronically Configurable Molecular-Based Logic Gates|journal=Science|date=16 July 1999|volume=285|issue=5426|pages=391–394|doi=10.1126/science.285.5426.391|pmid=10411498|citeseerx=10.1.1.474.5740}}</ref>

As of 2011, Heath's research has split into one area devoted to solid-state quantum physics, materials science, and surface science, with a slight focus on energy conversion and another working on applying synthetic chemistry and a systems perspective to fundamental biology and translational medicine - with a clear focus on [[oncology]].

== Awards and honours ==
Heath has received several awards and honours for his research.<ref name="UCLA2">{{cite web|title=James R. Heath|url=http://www.chem.ucla.edu/dept/Faculty/heath/|website=UCLA|accessdate=19 July 2016}}</ref> He was awarded the 2000 [[Feynman Prize in Nanotechnology]]. He became a fellow of [[American Physical Society]] in 1999.<ref name="APS">{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=H|website=APS Physics|accessdate=19 July 2016}}</ref> In 2009, Heath was named one of the seven most powerful innovators of the world by ''[[Forbes magazine]].''<ref name="Harper">{{cite news|last1=Harper|first1=Matthew|title=The Great Reaction|url=https://www.forbes.com/forbes/2009/1130/power-09-worlds-powerful-people-barry-sharpless-great-reaction.html|accessdate=19 July 2016|work=Forbes|date=November 12, 2009}}</ref>
